lessons.title: Multiplication Tables (2–10)
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Multiplication is one of the most useful skills in maths. We use it every day — when buying multiple items, calculating areas, and much more. The multiplication tables from 2 to 10 form the foundation of all advanced maths. The commutative property means 4×6 = 6×4 — the order doesn't change the answer!
practical_activities: Times table grid practise
Multiplication snap card game
Real-world multiplication problems

homework.task: Practise the 7× and 9× tables until perfect. Write each 10 times.

revision.notes: Learn all tables 2–10. Key: 9× trick (digits sum to 9). 7×8=56 (remember: 5,6,7,8).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Long Division
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Division is splitting a number into equal groups. 56 ÷ 7 = 8 means: 56 split into groups of 7 gives 8 groups. Long division: How many times does 7 go into 56? 7×8=56, so 8. Sometimes there's a remainder: 57 ÷ 7 = 8 remainder 1 (57 = 7×8 + 1).
practical_activities: Share objects equally into groups
Long division with remainders on whiteboards
Division word problem stations

revision.notes: Division: opposite of multiplication. Check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Fractions: Equivalence and Ordering
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Two fractions are equivalent if they represent the same amount. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 — these all equal exactly half! To find equivalent fractions, multiply (or divide) both numerator and denominator by the same number. To compare fractions with the same denominator, the bigger numerator wins.
practical_activities: Fraction walls comparison activity
Colour equivalent fraction grids
Order fraction strips from smallest to largest

homework.task: Find 3 fractions equivalent to 1/3. Draw fraction diagrams to prove it.

revision.notes: Equivalents: multiply top and bottom by same number. 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. Add same-denominator fractions by adding numerators.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Calculate perimeter of rectangles and squares
lessons.reading_material: PERIMETER is the distance around the outside of a shape — like a fence around a garden. AREA is the space inside a shape — like the grass inside the fence. Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + width). Area of a rectangle = length × width. A shape can have a big perimeter but small area, or vice versa!
practical_activities: Measure room perimeters with a trundle wheel
Count squares on grid paper for area
Design gardens on squared paper

homework.task: Measure the perimeter and area of 3 objects in your home using a ruler.

revision.notes: Perimeter = sum of all sides. Rectangle area = L × W. Units: cm for perimeter, cm² for area.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Decimals: Tenths
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Read and write decimal numbers to one decimal place
Understand tenths on a number line
lessons.reading_material: Decimals extend our number system beyond whole numbers. 0.1 means one tenth. The decimal point separates whole numbers from fractions. 3.7 means 3 whole and 7 tenths. On a number line, between 3 and 4 there are 10 equal spaces: 3.1, 3.2, 3.3...3.9. Money uses decimals: £2.50 means 2 pounds and 5 tenths.
practical_activities: Shade decimal grids
Place decimals on number lines
Convert fractions to decimals (1/10, 3/10)

homework.task: Write 5 temperatures (e.g. 36.5°C) as decimals and order them.

revision.notes: Decimals: tenths place is first after decimal point. 0.1 = 1/10. Compare by tenths digit.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Reading: Comprehension Strategies
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Identify main idea and supporting details
lessons.reading_material: Expert readers use STRATEGIES to understand texts better. PREDICTION: think ahead — what will happen next? INFERENCE: read between the lines — what does the author imply? VISUALISATION: create mental pictures. Main idea = the most important point. Supporting details = evidence for the main idea. SKIMMING: read quickly to get the gist. SCANNING: look for specific information.
practical_activities: Inference from picture clues
Skim a passage and state main idea
Scan for answers to questions

exercises.q: What is the main idea of a text?
exercises.answer: The most important point or overall topic

homework.task: Read a news article. Write: main idea (1 sentence) + 3 supporting details + your inference about the author's purpose.

revision.notes: Predict before/during. Infer: text clues + your knowledge. Main idea: often in first or last sentence. Scan for key words.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Food Chains
lessons.subject: Science
lessons.reading_material: A food chain shows who eats whom. Producers (plants) make their own food. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat plants. Secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores. Energy flows from sun → plant → herbivore → carnivore.
practical_activities: Build a food chain with cards
Create a food web poster

homework.task: Write a 3-step food chain you can find in your garden

revision.notes: Sun → Plant → Herbivore → Carnivore shows energy flow.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Forces: Push and Pull
lessons.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Give examples of push and pull forces in everyday life
lessons.reading_material: A force is a push or pull that changes an object's motion or shape. Pushing a door opens it. Pulling a drawer opens it. Gravity pulls everything towards Earth. Friction slows moving objects.
practical_activities: Experiment: push toy car — what changes?
Test friction on different surfaces

homework.task: List 5 examples of forces you experienced today

revision.notes: Force changes speed or direction. Friction always opposes motion.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Rivers and Landforms
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Describe how rivers shape the land
lessons.reading_material: Rivers begin at a source (often mountains) and end at a mouth (sea or lake). Along the way: upper course (fast, V-shaped valley), middle course (meanders), lower course (flood plain, delta). Rivers erode, transport, and deposit material.
practical_activities: Trace a river from source to mouth on a map
Build a model showing erosion with sand and water

homework.task: Research the Nile, Amazon, or Mississippi River — where does it start and end?

revision.notes: Source→Upper course→Middle course→Lower course→Mouth.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Population and Settlements
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Explain why people settle in certain places
lessons.reading_material: People settle near water, fertile land, and transportation routes. A village is a small settlement; a town is larger; a city is the largest. Urban areas have lots of people and services. Rural areas have fewer people and more farmland.
practical_activities: Compare aerial photos of a village and a city
Map the growth of a city over decades

homework.task: Find out the population of your nearest city

revision.notes: Urban = high density, many services. Rural = low density, mainly farming.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Fables and Their Lessons
lessons.subject: World Literature
learning_objectives: Read and interpret an Aesop fable
Identify the moral of a story

lessons.reading_material: Fables are short stories with animal characters that teach a moral lesson. Aesop (620–564 BCE), a Greek storyteller, wrote hundreds of fables. Famous examples: 'The Tortoise and the Hare' (slow and steady wins the race), 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf' (liars are not believed even when telling the truth). Panchatantra (India, 3rd century BCE) also uses animal fables for moral teaching. Jataka tales (Buddhist fables) feature the previous lives of the Buddha.
practical_activities: Write and illustrate a new fable with an original moral — share with the class
exercises: What is a fable?
State the moral of 'The Tortoise and the Hare'
Name one fable from a non-Greek culture
lessons.homework: Read one Panchatantra story and compare its moral to an Aesop fable.

revision.notes: Fable = short story with animal characters + moral lesson. Aesop (Greek), Panchatantra (Indian), Jataka (Buddhist).
revision.tip: Every fable has a hidden lesson — spot the human weakness each animal represents.

revision.notes: Every Good Boy Does Fine = E G B D F (lines). FACE = F A C E (spaces in the treble clef).

lessons.title: Personal Safety Basics
lessons.subject: Survival Skills
learning_objectives: Know their home address and emergency number
lessons.reading_material: Personal safety means protecting yourself from harm. Always know your home address and phone number. The emergency number in most countries is 999 (UK), 911 (USA), or 112 (international). If you feel unsafe, use the 'Stop, Think, Act' approach: Stop what you are doing, Think about the danger, Act by getting to a safe adult. Never go anywhere with a stranger. If separated from your family in public, find a police officer or shop worker.
practical_activities: Role play: what do you do if a stranger asks you to go with them?
exercises: What is the emergency number in your country?
Name 3 rules for staying safe in public
Who should you go to if you are lost?
lessons.homework: Memorise your home address and a parent's phone number — recite it without looking.

revision.notes: Know: home address, emergency number, Stop-Think-Act, trusted adults.
revision.tip: Practise saying your address aloud every day until it's automatic.

info_cards.title: Philosophical Quote
info_cards.fact: "The unexamined life is not worth living." — Socrates, ancient Greek philosopher.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "In the middle of difficulty lies opportunity." — Albert Einstein, physicist.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Albert Einstein
info_cards.fact: Albert Einstein developed the theory of relativity and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for his work on the photoelectric effect.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: The Diary of a Young Girl
info_cards.fact: "The Diary of a Young Girl" is the real wartime diary of Anne Frank, a Jewish teenager who hid with her family during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands; it remains one of the most widely read accounts of the Holocaust.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
info_cards.fact: "The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind" by William Kamkwamba tells how a teenager in Malawi built a windmill from scrap parts to bring electricity to his family's home.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: William Shakespeare
info_cards.fact: "All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players." — English playwright and poet widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Homer
info_cards.fact: "Sing in me, Muse, and through me tell the story." — Ancient Greek poet traditionally credited with composing the epic poems the Iliad and the Odyssey.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Confucius
info_cards.fact: "It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop." — Chinese philosopher and teacher whose ideas about ethics and good government shaped East Asian culture for centuries.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Socrates
info_cards.fact: "The only true wisdom is in knowing you know nothing." — Ancient Greek philosopher whose method of questioning laid the foundation for Western philosophy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Aristotle
info_cards.fact: "Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom." — Ancient Greek philosopher and scientist who studied logic, biology, and ethics, and tutored Alexander the Great.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Plato
info_cards.fact: "Wonder is the beginning of wisdom." — Ancient Greek philosopher who founded the Academy in Athens and wrote about justice and the ideal society.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Cleopatra VII
info_cards.fact: "I will not be triumphed over." — The last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, known for her intelligence and political skill.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Marco Polo
info_cards.fact: "I have not told half of what I saw." — Venetian merchant and explorer whose travels along the Silk Road to China were recorded in The Travels of Marco Polo.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ibn Battuta
info_cards.fact: "Travelling... leaves you speechless, then turns you into a storyteller." — Moroccan scholar who traveled across most of the medieval Islamic world and beyond, recording his journeys.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Zheng He
info_cards.fact: "We have traversed more than 100,000 li of immense water spaces." — Chinese admiral who led seven large naval expeditions across Southeast Asia, India, and East Africa in the 1400s.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Christopher Columbus
info_cards.fact: "You can never cross the ocean until you have the courage to lose sight of the shore." — Italian explorer whose 1492 voyage across the Atlantic opened sustained European contact with the Americas.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ferdinand Magellan
info_cards.fact: "We were more starved than any people ever were." — Portuguese explorer whose expedition completed the first circumnavigation of the globe (1519-1522).

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Vasco da Gama
info_cards.fact: "I am not bound to please thee with my answers." — Portuguese explorer who led the first European voyage by sea from Europe to India, opening a new trade route.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Johannes Gutenberg
info_cards.fact: "Religious truth is imprisoned in a small number of manuscript books... Let us break the seal which seals up holy things." — German inventor credited with creating the printing press with movable type in Europe, transforming the spread of books.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Charlemagne
info_cards.fact: "To have another language is to possess a second soul." — King of the Franks crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800 CE, who reunited much of Western Europe under one rule.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Joan of Arc
info_cards.fact: "I am not afraid... I was born to do this." — French peasant girl who led French troops to several victories during the Hundred Years' War.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Genghis Khan
info_cards.fact: "Conquering the world on horseback is easy. It is dismounting and governing that is hard." — Mongol leader who founded the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Suleiman the Magnificent
info_cards.fact: "I, who am the sultan of sultans... give these orders." — Ottoman sultan whose reign in the 16th century marked the empire's peak in power, wealth, and culture.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Akbar the Great
info_cards.fact: "Pursue justice and reason in all things." — Mughal emperor of India known for religious tolerance and uniting much of the Indian subcontinent.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Saladin
info_cards.fact: "I have become an army without a country." — Muslim sultan of Egypt and Syria who led the Muslim military campaign against the Crusader states.

lessons.title: Kitchen Safety and Hygiene
lessons.subject: Cooking
lessons.reading_material: The kitchen can be a dangerous place if we are not careful. Sharp knives must be handled by adults. Hot surfaces can cause burns. Always wash your hands for at least 20 seconds before handling food. Keep raw meat away from other foods to prevent contamination. Store food at the right temperature — bacteria grow quickly between 5°C and 60°C (the 'danger zone'). Always clean surfaces before and after cooking.
practical_activities: Practise hand-washing with soap and time it at 20 seconds; identify hazards in a kitchen photo
exercises: Name 3 kitchen hazards and how to avoid each

lessons.homework: Design a 'Kitchen Safety Rules' poster with 5 illustrated rules.

revision.notes: Danger zone = 5°C–60°C. Wash hands 20 sec. Separate raw and cooked foods.
revision.tip: Colour-coded chopping boards (red = meat, green = vegetables) prevent cross-contamination.

lessons.title: Colours and Animals in Arabic
lessons.subject: Foreign Languages
learning_objectives: Use simple sentences: 'The cat is red'
lessons.reading_material: Colours in Arabic: أحمر (red), أزرق (blue), أصفر (yellow), أخضر (green), أبيض (white), أسود (black), برتقالي (orange), وردي (pink). Animals: قطة (cat), كلب (dog), أسد (lion), فيل (elephant), طائر (bird), سمكة (fish), حصان (horse), فراشة (butterfly). Sentence: القطة حمراء (The cat is red).
practical_activities: Flashcard race: hold up colour/animal flashcards and students call out Arabic word
exercises: Write 5 colour words in Arabic
Translate: 'The lion is yellow' into Arabic
Draw 5 animals and label them in Arabic
lessons.homework: Draw 8 coloured objects and write the Arabic colour word next to each.

revision.notes: Colours and animals are core vocabulary. Sentence pattern: Subject + Adjective (القطة حمراء).
revision.tip: Group colours by theme (warm: red/orange/yellow; cool: blue/green) to memorise faster.

lessons.assessment: Write 5 sentences in Arabic using an animal and a colour in each.

lessons.title: Maps and Geography Skills
lessons.subject: Social Studies
learning_objectives: Read a simple map using a key
Locate features on a local map
lessons.reading_material: A map is a drawing that shows an area from above. Maps have a key (legend) that explains symbols used. Cardinal directions — North, South, East, West — help us describe location. A compass shows direction. Scale tells us how real distances relate to map distances. Maps help us navigate, plan journeys, and understand places. Different types of maps exist: physical maps (landforms), political maps (countries), and climate maps.
practical_activities: Create a map of your classroom using symbols and a key
exercises: Draw a compass rose and label N, S, E, W
What does a map key tell us?
If 1 cm = 10 km on a map, how far is 5 cm in reality?
lessons.homework: Draw a map of your route to school, including a key and directional arrow.

revision.notes: Map key = symbols explained. Cardinal directions = N, S, E, W. Scale shows real distance.
revision.tip: Memorise: 'Never Eat Soggy Waffles' for N, E, S, W clockwise.

quiz.question: What does a map KEY show?

lessons.assessment: Read a given map and answer 5 questions about location, direction, and distance.
textbook_references: Oxford Primary Geography — Oxford University Press

lessons.title: Protecting Our Environment
lessons.subject: Environmental Science
learning_objectives: Explain why the environment needs protection
lessons.reading_material: The environment is everything around us: air, water, soil, plants, and animals. Pollution harms the environment: litter, car exhaust, factory waste. We can help: reduce (use less), reuse (use again), recycle (make into new things). Plant trees. Save water and electricity.
practical_activities: Sort materials for recycling
Calculate personal water usage for one day

homework.task: Keep a litter log for one week — pick up 3 pieces of litter per day

revision.notes: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle = 3Rs. Everyone can protect the environment through daily choices.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Team Games and Sportsmanship
lessons.subject: Physical Education & Self-Defense
lessons.reading_material: Team sports teach cooperation, communication, and fairness. Sportsmanship: play fairly, respect opponents and referees, win graciously, lose graciously. Cooperation: pass, communicate, support teammates. Sports like football, basketball, and rounders build fitness and teamwork.
practical_activities: Play a mini football or basketball game
Discuss: what is good and bad sportsmanship?

homework.task: Reflect: describe a time you showed good sportsmanship

revision.notes: Good sportsmanship = fair play + respect + grace in winning and losing.

lessons.title: Balanced Diet and the Food Plate
lessons.subject: Health Education
learning_objectives: Explain why each food group is important
lessons.reading_material: A balanced diet includes all five food groups: grains (energy), protein (muscle building), dairy (bones and teeth), fruits and vegetables (vitamins and minerals), and healthy fats in moderation. The food plate shows roughly how much of each group to eat.
practical_activities: Sort food picture cards into food groups
Design a balanced lunchbox
exercises: Name a food from each of the 5 food groups
Explain why we should limit sugar
lessons.homework: Plan 3 balanced meals for one day, making sure all food groups are included.

revision.notes: Half your plate should be fruits and vegetables — colour means vitamins!
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which food group provides the main source of energy?

lessons.assessment: Create a balanced meal plan for one full day with food group annotations.

lessons.title: Introduction to Programming: Scratch
lessons.subject: ICT & Computer Science
learning_objectives: Create a simple Scratch project with sequences
lessons.reading_material: An algorithm is a set of step-by-step instructions. In Scratch, you drag blocks to make a sprite move, speak, or change. A sequence runs blocks in order. Loops repeat blocks. Events start a sequence (e.g., when green flag clicked).
practical_activities: Create a Scratch project: make a sprite walk across screen
Design an algorithm to make a sandwich (unplugged)

homework.task: Build a Scratch animation where a character says hello and moves

revision.notes: Algorithm = steps. Sequence = in order. Loop = repeat. Scratch uses visual blocks.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class
